original_interpretation: CSET judged that US firms other than Intel lack high-volume packaging capacity and that the associated US ecosystem (substrates, wafer bumping, equipment) is also lacking.
evidence_found: "In general, U.S. firms (with the exception of Intel) lack high-volume packaging capacity, and the associated ecosystem (substrates, wafer bumping, equipment) is also lacking." (CSET, Re-Shoring Advanced Semiconductor Packaging, June 2022, p. 17, 'U.S. Policy and Advanced Packaging')
notes: Attributed judgment dated June 2022; since then Amkor (Peoria, AZ) and others have begun US high-volume packaging builds (see CLM-1060, CLM-1063), so the judgment should be read as a 2022 snapshot.

original_interpretation: The SEMI/TechSearch International Worldwide Assembly & Test Facility Database (March 2024 edition) covers 670 facilities: 500 OSAT facilities and 170 IDM assembly and test facilities.
evidence_found: "670 facilities, 33% more than the previous release, including 500 outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) service providers and 170 integrated device manufacturer (IDM) facilities" (3D InCites republication of SEMI/TechSearch release, 18 Mar 2024)
correction: Accurate for the March 2024 edition, but superseded: the 2026 edition (SEMI/TechSearch release, 7 Jul 2026) covers "more than 820 facilities, up from 750 in the 2025 edition"; the 2026 release does not give an OSAT/IDM split.

original_interpretation: The 2024 SEMI/TechSearch database lists more than 150 OSAT and about 45 IDM back-end facilities in China, 130-plus OSAT facilities in Taiwan, and more than 60 OSAT and 50-plus IDM facilities in Southeast Asia.
evidence_found: "130-plus OSAT facilities in Taiwan, more than 150 in China, and more than 60 in Southeast Asia"; "50-plus IDM assembly and test facilities in Southeast Asia, about 45 in China, nearly 20 in Americas and more than 12 in Europe" (3D InCites / SEMI-TechSearch release, 18 Mar 2024)
notes: Counts are for the 2024 edition; the 2026 edition (820+ facilities) does not publish regional counts in its release, and says the largest additions were in Mainland China and Taiwan.

original_interpretation: The 2024 SEMI/TechSearch database lists nearly 20 IDM assembly and test facilities in the Americas and more than 12 in Europe.
evidence_found: "... nearly 20 in Americas and more than 12 in Europe" (IDM assembly and test facilities; 3D InCites / SEMI-TechSearch release, 18 Mar 2024)

original_interpretation: In the 2024 SEMI/TechSearch database, more than 30% of back-end factories offer advanced packaging, with 85-plus bumping facilities, 90-plus WLCSP facilities, 100-plus QFN facilities and 325-plus facilities with test capability.
evidence_found: "More than 30% of global factories offering advanced packaging capabilities in one of the following areas: flip chip bumping and assembly, fan-out and fan-in WLP, TSV, 2.5D and 3D"; "85-plus bumping facilities, including more than 65 with 300mm wafer bumping capacity"; "90-plus facilities offering WLCSP technology"; "100-plus facilities offering QFN"; "325-plus facilities with test capabilities" (3D InCites / SEMI-TechSearch release, 18 Mar 2024)
notes: 2024 edition counts; facility counts, not capacity.

original_interpretation: Southeast Asia is where IDMs keep much of their own back-end: the SEMI/TechSearch database lists 50-plus IDM assembly/test sites there versus about 45 in China and fewer than 20 in the Americas.
evidence_found: Release gives IDM A&T facilities: "50-plus ... in Southeast Asia, about 45 in China, nearly 20 in Americas and more than 12 in Europe" (3D InCites, 18 Mar 2024). No IDM counts for Japan, South Korea or Taiwan.
correction: The counts are correctly read, but the listed regions total roughly 127 of 170 IDM facilities; about 40 IDM facilities (likely Japan, Korea, Taiwan and others) are not broken out, so Southeast Asia is the largest of the listed regions, not demonstrably the largest overall. 'Fewer than 20' should read 'nearly 20' for the Americas. Facility counts are not capacity.

original_interpretation: Amkor's 2025 net sales were US$5,556 million (82.8%) from 'advanced products' (flip chip, memory, wafer-level processing and related test) and US$1,152 million (17.2%) from 'mainstream products' (wirebond and power-device packaging and related test).
evidence_found: "We refer to our flip chip, memory, wafer-level processing and related test services as 'Advanced Products' and to our wirebond packaging, power device packaging and related test services as 'Mainstream Products.'" Table: "Advanced Products $ 5,556 82.8 % ... Mainstream Products 1,152 17.2 % ... Total net sales $ 6,708" (Amkor Form 10-K FY2025, Item 1, Advanced Products and Mainstream Products)

original_interpretation: Amkor's 2025 net sales by end market were communications 46%, computing 20%, automotive/industrial/other 19% and consumer 15%.
evidence_found: "End Market Distribution Data (an approximation including representative devices and applications based on a sampling of our largest customers): Communications (smartphones, tablets) 46 % ... Computing (data center, infrastructure, PC/laptop, storage) 20 % ... Automotive, industrial and other (ADAS, electrification, infotainment, safety) 19 % ... Consumer (AR & gaming, connected home, home electronics, wearables) 15 %" (Amkor Form 10-K FY2025, Item 1, End Markets; same figures in Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements)
notes: Item 1 labels the split an approximation based on a sampling of largest customers; metric methodology should say so.

original_interpretation: Amkor states that chip companies outsource packaging and test because providers bring advanced-technology expertise, shorten time-to-market, let chipmakers focus capital on design and wafer fabrication, and achieve better asset utilisation across many customers in a cyclical, capital-intensive industry.
evidence_found: "Packaging and test service providers can facilitate a more efficient supply chain and help shorten time-to-market for new products."; "High quality packaging and test service providers enable semiconductor manufacturers to focus their resources on semiconductor design and wafer fabrication."; "Packaging and test service providers offer a cost-effective solution in a cyclical, capital intensive industry."; "Packaging and test service providers, on the other hand, can typically use their assets to support a broad range of customers and multiple end markets, potentially generating more efficient use of their production assets" (Amkor Form 10-K FY2025, Item 1, industry/outsourcing section)

original_interpretation: Amkor describes itself as the world's largest US-headquartered OSAT.
evidence_found: "Amkor is the world's largest U.S. headquartered outsourced semiconductor assembly and test service provider ('OSAT')" (Amkor Form 10-K FY2025, Item 1. Business, Overview)

original_interpretation: Amkor opened a factory in Vietnam in 2024 and began construction of a new facility in Arizona in the second half of 2025.
evidence_found: "As a U.S. headquartered OSAT, we are expanding our manufacturing footprint with the construction of a new facility in Arizona. Construction began in the second half of 2025 ... In addition, we continue to scale production in our Vietnam facility, which opened in 2024" (Amkor Form 10-K FY2025, Item 1)

original_interpretation: The US Department of Commerce awarded Amkor Technology Arizona up to US$407 million in CHIPS direct funding (December 2024) to support an investment of about US$2 billion in a greenfield advanced packaging and test facility in Peoria, Arizona, expected to create about 2,000 manufacturing jobs.
evidence_found: NIST release (20 Dec 2024): award of "up to $407 million in direct funding" to Amkor Technology Arizona, Inc.; investment of "approximately $2 billion" in Peoria, Arizona; "an estimated 2,000 manufacturing jobs" (plus more than 2,000 construction jobs at peak)

original_interpretation: US Commerce framed the Amkor Arizona award as ending the need to send US-made chips overseas for packaging after fabrication.
evidence_found: "Advanced packaging is a critical part of the semiconductor supply chain, and bringing this capability to the U.S. will mean chips don't need to be sent overseas after they have been manufactured." (Secretary Raimondo, NIST release, 20 Dec 2024)
notes: A policy framing by the Secretary, quoted accurately; not evidence that overseas packaging need ends.

original_interpretation: In October 2025 Amkor broke ground on its Peoria, Arizona campus and raised the planned investment from US$2 billion to US$7 billion across two phases, with over 750,000 sq ft of cleanroom and up to 3,000 jobs.
evidence_found: Amkor release (6 Oct 2025, via AnySilicon), headline 'Amkor Technology Breaks Ground on New Semiconductor Advanced Packaging and Test Campus in Arizona; Expands Investment to $7 Billion': investment "$7 billion" across two phases (up from $2 billion); "over 750,000 square feet of cleanroom space"; approximately 3,000 jobs

original_interpretation: Amkor expects construction of the first Arizona facility to finish in mid-2027 with production starting in early 2028, serving customers including Apple and NVIDIA alongside TSMC's Arizona wafer fabrication.
evidence_found: Amkor release (6 Oct 2025, via AnySilicon): construction completion "mid-2027"; production start "early 2028"; Apple and NVIDIA named as customers, complementing TSMC's Arizona wafer fabrication

original_interpretation: Amkor describes its Arizona campus as the first US-based high-volume advanced packaging facility.
evidence_found: "first U.S. based high volume advanced packaging facility" (Amkor release, 6 Oct 2025, via AnySilicon)

original_interpretation: By August 2025 the India Semiconductor Mission had approved 10 projects with cumulative investment of about Rs 1.60 lakh crore in 6 states.
evidence_found: "Total approved projects under ISM reaches to 10 with cumulative investments of around Rs.1.60 lakh crore in 6 states." (PIB, 'Powering the Future: The Semiconductor and AI Revolution', 15 Aug 2025, p. 1, Major Milestones)

original_interpretation: India approved Micron Technology's ATMP facility at Sanand, Gujarat in June 2023 with an investment of Rs 22,516 crore.
evidence_found: "JUN 2023 Micron Technology Sanand, Gujarat ₹22,516 crore ATMP Facility, with phased ramp-up." (PIB, 15 Aug 2025, p. 2, Approved Plants table)

original_interpretation: India approved Tata Semiconductor Assembly and Test (TSAT) at Morigaon, Assam in February 2024 with an investment of Rs 27,000 crore and a capacity of 48 million chips per day.
evidence_found: "FEB 2024 Tata Semiconductor Assembly and Test Pvt Ltd (TSAT) Morigaon, Assam ₹27,000 crore 48 million chips/day" (PIB, 15 Aug 2025, p. 2)

original_interpretation: India approved a CG Power unit with Renesas and Stars Microelectronics at Sanand, Gujarat in February 2024 with an investment of about Rs 7,600 crore and capacity of 15 million chips per day.
evidence_found: "FEB 2024 CG Power & Industrial Pvt Ltd in partnership with Renasas and Stars Sanand, Gujarat ~₹7,600 crore 15 million chips/day" (PIB, 15 Aug 2025, p. 2)

original_interpretation: India approved Kaynes Semicon at Sanand, Gujarat in September 2024 with an investment of Rs 3,307 crore and capacity of 6.33 million chips per day.
evidence_found: "SEPT 2024 Kaynes Semicon Pvt Ltd Sanand, Gujarat ₹3,307 crore 6.33 million chips/day" (PIB, 15 Aug 2025, p. 2)

original_interpretation: In August 2025 India approved four more units with back-end components: SiCSem (Odisha, Rs 2,066 crore, incl. ATMP of 96 million units/yr), 3D Glass Solutions (Odisha, Rs 1,943 crore, ATMP 50 million units/yr), CDIL (Mohali, Rs 117 crore, 158 million units/yr) and ASIP (Andhra Pradesh, Rs 468 crore, 96 million units/yr).
evidence_found: PIB table p. 3 (AUGUST 2025 rows): "SicSem ... ₹2,066 crore 60 thousand wafers per year; ATMP capacity: 96 million Units/year"; "3D Glass Solutions Inc. ... ₹1,943 Cr Glass panels: 70 Thousand units/year; ATMP : 50 million units/ year"; "CDIL (Continental Device) Mohali, Punjab ₹117 Cr 158 million units /year"; "ASIP (Advanced System in Package Technologies) Andhra Pradesh ₹468 Cr 96 million units /year". Cabinet coverage (Governance Now, 12 Aug 2025) describes CDIL as a brownfield "discrete semiconductor manufacturing facility at Mohali" for "MOSFETs, IGBTs, Schottky Bypass Diodes, and transistors".
correction: Figures are correct, but the PIB table does not label CDIL or ASIP as ATMP; CDIL is a brownfield discrete-device manufacturing expansion (158.38 million units/yr), so calling all four 'units with back-end components' overstates what the source says for CDIL. ASIP's back-end character is suggested by its name and partner (APACT) but not stated in the table.

original_interpretation: Of India's first 10 ISM-approved projects, 8 are assembly/test (ATMP/OSAT) or include an ATMP line, and only 2 (Tata-PSMC Dholera and HCL-Foxconn Jewar) are pure wafer fabs, so India's entry is back-end-led.
evidence_found: PIB table (15 Aug 2025, pp. 2-3) lists the 10 plants; HCL-Foxconn row: "MAY 2025 HCL-Foxconn JV Jewar, Uttar Pradesh ₹3,700 crore 20,000 wafers/month (36 M units/yr)". TechCrunch (14 May 2025): the Jewar unit will "at first, be used as a semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) facility. That means it will be focused on providing packaging and testing services for chips that have been manufactured elsewhere".
correction: HCL-Foxconn Jewar was reported at approval as initially an OSAT (packaging/test of wafers made elsewhere), not a pure wafer fab; CDIL is a brownfield discrete-device manufacturing expansion not labelled ATMP. Tata-PSMC Dholera is the only unambiguous wafer fab. The 'back-end-led' conclusion holds, but the 8/2 split and the naming of HCL-Foxconn as a fab do not. See superseding claim.

original_interpretation: In May 2026 India approved two further projects with over INR 39 billion (about US$400 million) combined: a Crystal Matrix compound-semiconductor fab and ATMP at Dholera and a Suchi Semicon OSAT for discrete semiconductors at Surat.
evidence_found: "Crystal Matrix Limited (CML) will establish an integrated facility for compound semiconductor fabrication and ATMP in Dholera, Gujarat"; "Suchi Semicon Private Limited (SSPL) will be setting up an OSAT facility in Surat, Gujarat, for manufacturing discrete semiconductors"; "a cumulative investment of over INR 39 billion (about USD 400 million)" (Evertiq, 7 May 2026)
notes: Tier-2 trade press relaying a government approval; the primary PIB/Cabinet release was not opened.

original_interpretation: Micron opened its Sanand, India assembly and test plant, which converts DRAM and NAND wafers into finished memory products, in February 2026; it has started commercial production and made its first shipment of India-made memory modules to Dell.
evidence_found: "Micron Technology has opened its first semiconductor test and assembly facility in Sanand, Gujarat"; "The facility converts advanced DRAM and NAND wafers from Micron's global manufacturing network into finished memory and storage products." The article reports the ISO-certified site has begun commercial operations and made its first shipment of India-made memory modules to Dell Technologies (Computer Weekly, published 02 Mar 2026 9:55). The article gives no opening date.
correction: The cited article (2 Mar 2026) supports the opening, function, commercial production and Dell shipment but does not state the month of opening. Search results (Micron/GlobeNewswire headline dated 2026-02-28 and PM Modi's 28 Feb Gujarat visit notice) point to a 28 Feb 2026 inauguration, but no opened page confirmed the date verbatim.

original_interpretation: Micron expects to assemble and test tens of millions of chips at Sanand in 2026 and hundreds of millions in 2027, with over 500,000 sq ft of cleanroom once phase one is fully ramped and a combined investment of about US$2.75 billion with government partners.
evidence_found: "Once fully ramped up, the first phase of the Sanand operation will feature more than 500,000 ft2 of cleanroom space"; "a combined investment of about $2.75bn by the chipmaker and its government partners"; expects to "test and assemble tens of millions of chips" in 2026 and "hundreds of millions in 2027" (Computer Weekly, 2 Mar 2026)

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG put the global assembly, test and packaging (ATP) market at US$95 billion, including both IDM in-house facilities and OSATs.
evidence_found: "The $95 billion ATP market is currently concentrated in Northeast Asia."; "(including both IDM ATP facilities and OSATs)" (SIA/BCG, Emerging Resilience in the Semiconductor Supply Chain, May 2024, p. 20)
notes: The report does not state the year of the $95bn figure.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG estimated conventional packaging at US$51 billion of the US$95 billion ATP market, and said the term 'advanced packaging' describes about 46% of the ATP market.
evidence_found: "Conventional packaging, which accounts for $51 billion of the $95 billion ATP market, is concentrated in developing countries, due to both the labor-intensive nature of the work and low margins." (p. 20); "While this term is used to describe approximately 46% of the ATP market" (p. 21, Sidebar: Chiplets)

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG estimated that mainland China and Taiwan together host nearly 60% of global ATP capacity (IDM and OSAT facilities combined).
evidence_found: "More importantly, Mainland China and Taiwan together host nearly 60% of global ATP capacity (including both IDM ATP facilities and OSATs)." (SIA/BCG 2024, p. 20)
notes: The sentence gives no year; the metric period '2022' is inferred from Exhibit 13 (2022-2032F), whose baseline is 2022.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG counted 36 ATP facilities announced since 2020, of which 25 are in mainland China and Taiwan (14 in China and 11 in Taiwan per the exhibit).
evidence_found: "Out of 36 ATP facilities announced since 2020, 25 are projected to be in Mainland China and Taiwan (see Exhibit 12)." Exhibit 12 'New ATP investments by region, 2020-2023' (p. 20): "Facilities 14 11 13" under Mainland China / Taiwan / Rest of World; the named facilities listed are 14 in mainland China, 11 in Taiwan and 13 in rest of world.
correction: The 25 = 14 (mainland China) + 11 (Taiwan) split is correct, but Exhibit 12 lists 38 facilities (14+11+13), not the 36 stated in the text; the source is internally inconsistent on the total.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG estimated Southeast Asia at about 20% of global ATP capacity, with Malaysia holding the largest share in the region.
evidence_found: "Southeast Asia is already home to significant ATP activity, accounting for ~20% of total global ATP capacity, with Malaysia capturing the greatest share within the region." (SIA/BCG 2024, p. 20)

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG forecast emerging-market ATP capacity (outside the US, Japan, Korea, China, Taiwan and EU) to rise from 20% of global capacity in 2022 to 27% in 2032, driven mainly by Southeast Asia.
evidence_found: "We forecast significant ATP capacity additions in these emerging markets, from 20% of global capacity in 2022 to 27% in 2032, primarily driven by Southeast Asia (see Exhibit 13)." (SIA/BCG 2024, p. 20; Exhibit 13 p. 21 splits capacity into US, Korea, Mainland China, Japan, Taiwan, EU and Others)

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG projected Vietnam's share of global ATP capacity to rise from less than 1% to 9% by 2032.
evidence_found: "Now Vietnam, a relative newcomer, is also attracting investments from Intel, Amkor, and other companies from around the world, and is projected to increase its share of global ATP capacity from less than 1% to 9% of global ATP capacity by 2032." (SIA/BCG 2024, p. 23); endnote 25: "Intel's IDM ATP facility in Vietnam is ~50,000 sq. meters of facility space (<1% of global ATP capacity) but ... we project Vietnam to reach 9% of world ATP capacity by 2032."
notes: Passage is on printed p. 23, not p. 22.
